body:
OBJECTIVES
- Students compute unit rates, including rates built from fractions, such as miles per hour from a fraction of a mile in a fraction of an hour (7.RP.A.1).
- Students decide whether two quantities are proportional using tables, graphs and equations, identify the constant of proportionality and explain what the point (1, k) means (7.RP.A.2).
- Students use proportional relationships to solve multistep ratio and percent problems: tax, tips, discounts, markups, simple interest, percent increase and percent error (7.RP.A.3).

MATERIALS
- Is It Proportional? (student overview), projected or printed
- Graph paper and rulers
- A class anchor chart with three columns: Table, Graph, Equation
- Calculators for the percent assignment (not for the unit check)
- Store flyers or menus you write yourself with prices, for the percent warm-up

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read Is It Proportional? together. Warm-up: is the cost of apples at $2 per pound proportional to the weight? Build a table and graph as a class. Begin the lesson Finding k: Tables, Graphs and Equations, problems 1-3.
Day 2: Finish the lesson (problems 4-5). Students explain what (1, k) means on two different graphs. Assign Unit Rates and the Constant of Proportionality, problem 1 in class.
Day 3: Finish Unit Rates and the Constant of Proportionality. Mini-lesson on percents as proportional relationships: a 25% discount means you pay 75%. Begin Percent Problems: Tax, Tips and Discounts.
Day 4: Finish Percent Problems. Pairs compare their answer to problem 5 (the markup and discount): why is the sale price not back to $30? Review the anchor chart.
Day 5: Assessment: Proportional or Not? Unit Check, without calculators. Students who finish early write a second real-life example of a non-proportional relationship.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: provide a table template with a y ÷ x column already drawn, so students can test each row. Let students use a double number line for unit rates.
- Support: for percent problems, offer the 10% strategy first (find 10%, then build 20%, 5% or 15%) before moving to decimal multipliers.
- Stretch/Extension: ask students to write one situation for each of y = 0.75x, y = 1.06x and y = x + 3, and explain which are proportional and why.
- Multilingual learners: pre-teach constant, ratio, rate, origin, discount, tax and tip with a picture or sketch for each. Accept explanations that combine a labeled table or graph with a short sentence, and offer the frame "This is proportional because ___."

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
This unit, your child is learning about proportional relationships: two amounts that grow at the same rate, like the cost of gas and the number of gallons. They will find unit rates ("how much for one?") and use percents for tax, tips and sale prices. At the store or a restaurant, ask your child to estimate a 20% tip or a 25%-off price before you pay. Asking "How much is that for one?" is the heart of this unit.
title: Teacher guide: Unit 2: Proportional Relationships
